q: Optical illusions result from distortion in:

concept.t: An optical illusion is a gap between what is really there and what we experience. In the Muller-Lyer figure, two equal lines look unequal.
The receptors register the lines correctly; the error arises when the brain interprets them. Interpreting input is the job of perception.
Sensation is detection and transduction; perception is organising and interpreting. Illusions are errors of the second step.

wrong.a: Not a stage of sensory processing at all; it is a distractor that sounds like transduction.
wrong.b: Sensation (detection and transduction) is accurate in an illusion: the receptors register the lines correctly.
wrong.d: Adaptation is the fading of response to a constant stimulus, not a misreading of a figure.

q: According to the Bayesian approach to perception, our perceptual experiences are influenced by:
who: Bayesian inference: prior combined with likelihood

concept.t: The Bayesian approach treats perception as a best guess. It combines the prior (what we expect) with the likelihood (what the senses report).
Each source is weighted by its reliability: clear sensory input counts for more, and when input is noisy the prior counts for more.

wrong.a: Genes may shape a person's priors, but they alone do not define the approach.
wrong.b: Culture may shape a person's priors, but it alone does not define the approach, which is prior plus sensory evidence.
wrong.d: Emotion may shape a person's priors, but it alone does not define the approach.

q: Who among the following has defined perception as a complex of sensory and imaginal events?

concept.t: For the structuralist Titchener, a perception was sensations plus the images that past experience attaches to them: a complex of sensory and imaginal events.
Structuralism broke consciousness into elements such as sensations and images, so a perception had to be built out of them.

wrong.a: A distractor name; not linked to this definition of perception.
wrong.c: Bruner is known for the New Look emphasis on needs and expectations in perception (Chapter 4), not this structuralist definition.
wrong.d: A distractor name; not linked to this definition of perception.

q: The minimum level of a stimulus that can be detected is called the:

concept.t: The absolute threshold is the weakest stimulus a person can detect. In practice it is the level detected on 50 percent of trials.
The absolute threshold asks "is anything there?"; the difference threshold asks "has it changed?".

wrong.a: The difference threshold (JND) is the smallest detectable change between stimuli, not the weakest detectable stimulus.
wrong.c: An invented term; no threshold goes by this name.
wrong.d: An invented term; it is not used in psychophysics.

q: The point at which a stimulus becomes strong enough to trigger a response only 50% of the time is:

concept.t: Detection does not switch on at one exact intensity; it rises gradually along the psychometric function. So thresholds are defined as 50 percent points.
The level that triggers a response half the time is the threshold of response.

wrong.b: Response bias is the signal detection term for an observer's readiness to say "yes"; a decision tendency, not a stimulus level.
wrong.c: A garbled mix of terms; signal detection theory replaces the fixed threshold with sensitivity and response bias.
wrong.d: The phi phenomenon is apparent movement between flashing lights (Wertheimer, 1912), not a threshold.

q: Every Just Noticeable Difference in stimulation constitutes a constant increment in sensation magnitude. Who among the following had given this assumption?

concept.t: Weber discovered that the JND is a constant fraction of the standard stimulus.
Fechner added the assumption that every JND is an equal step of sensation. Adding up those equal steps, he derived his logarithmic law.

wrong.a: Ebbinghaus applied Fechner's methods to memory; he made no claim about JNDs as steps of sensation.
wrong.b: Weber found the JND is a constant fraction of the standard; the equal-step assumption was Fechner's addition. Classic trap.
wrong.c: Tolman was a learning theorist (purposive behaviourism, cognitive maps), not a psychophysicist.

q: In signal detection theory, the ability to distinguish a stimulus from background noise is:

concept.t: d′ is the separation between the noise and signal-plus-noise distributions. The further apart they are, the easier the signal is to pick out.
d′ does not depend on willingness to say "yes", so it measures ability, not bias.

wrong.b: The criterion (β) is the willingness to say "yes" (response bias), not the ability to detect.
wrong.c: The ROC curve is the plot of hit rate against false alarm rate; a graph, not the ability itself.
wrong.d: The JND belongs to classical psychophysics, not signal detection theory.

q: "Receiver-operant characteristics" in communication studies refer to:

concept.t: In communication research the receiver is the audience. Receiver characteristics such as self-esteem, involvement and initial attitude moderate persuasion (Social Psychology book).
The wording echoes the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve of signal detection theory, which is a different idea.

wrong.a: Bait for confusion with the ROC curve of signal detection theory; auditory thresholds are psychophysics, not communication studies.
wrong.b: Plays on the word "operant", but receiver factors are audience traits, not reinforcement of recall.
wrong.c: Too narrow: receiver factors are audience traits (self-esteem, involvement, initial attitude) that moderate persuasion, not biases in decoding a message.

q: The visible spectrum wavelength ranges from:

concept.t: The visible spectrum is the band of wavelengths the human eye can see, about 380 to 760 nanometres.
Shorter wavelengths are ultraviolet and longer ones infrared, both invisible to humans.
Some books round the range to 400 to 700 nanometres, but no option offers that.

wrong.b: Starts at 200 nm, inside the ultraviolet, which humans cannot see.
wrong.c: Runs to 1000 nm, into the infrared, which humans cannot see.
wrong.d: Includes both ultraviolet and infrared; far too wide.

q: What is the relationship between frequency and wavelength?

concept.t: Speed equals frequency multiplied by wavelength.
For light or sound travelling at a fixed speed, a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength, so the two are inversely related.

wrong.a: Wrong direction: at a fixed speed, a higher frequency gives a shorter wavelength, so they move in opposite directions.
wrong.b: Not a mathematical relationship; a distractor.
wrong.c: Not a mathematical relationship; a distractor.

q: Which of the following act as receptor(s) for scotopic vision?

concept.t: Scotopic vision is dim-light vision. It depends on the rods and their pigment rhodopsin.
Cones serve photopic (daylight, colour) vision.

wrong.a: The retina is the tissue that contains both receptor types; it is not itself the receptor.
wrong.b: Cones serve photopic (daylight, colour) vision, not dim-light vision.
wrong.c: The iris controls the pupil; it is not a receptor.

concept.t: Cones provide colour vision through three pigments. It is the rods, with one pigment, that give colourless (monochromatic) vision.
In an INCORRECT item the other options are true; here the other three statements are true of cones.

wrong.a: True: cones are packed most densely in the fovea, at the centre of the retina.
wrong.b: True: cones need moderate to bright light, which is why they serve photopic (daylight) vision.
wrong.d: True: little convergence (few cones feed each ganglion cell) gives cones sharp acuity for fine detail.

q: Dark adaptation is the process in which the eyes get more sensitive to:
who: Dark adaptation, rhodopsin regeneration in rods

concept.t: In darkness, regeneration of rhodopsin makes the rods thousands of times more sensitive over about 30 minutes.
The eye becomes far more sensitive to light with low illumination; that is what dark adaptation means.

wrong.a: Although rods are most sensitive to blue-green, "green light" misses the point: dark adaptation raises sensitivity to dim light in general.
wrong.b: Dark-adapted rods are colour-blind, so sensitivity to coloured lights is not what improves.
wrong.c: Becoming adjusted to bright light is light adaptation, the reverse process.

q: The process of getting adjusted to different intensities of light is called:
who: Visual adaptation: dark and light adaptation

concept.t: Visual adaptation adjusts the eye's sensitivity to the light level.
It works both ways: dark adaptation in dim light and light adaptation in bright light.

wrong.b: Assimilation belongs to Piaget's theory of cognitive development, not vision.
wrong.c: Accommodation is the lens changing shape to focus, not adjusting to light intensity.
wrong.d: Sensation is the general detection of stimuli, not the specific adjustment to light levels.

q: The Mach bands phenomenon is best explained by:
who: Lateral inhibition in the retina, Mach bands

concept.t: Mach bands are illusory light and dark bands seen along the edge between two shades.
Neighbouring retinal cells inhibit each other (lateral inhibition), exaggerating contrast at edges and producing the bands.

wrong.a: Wrong anatomy: the fovea contains no rods at all, so there is no rod-cone split there.
wrong.b: The opponent-process theory explains colour afterimages, not brightness bands at edges.
wrong.d: Temporal summation is the adding together of weak signals over time, not contrast between neighbouring regions.

concept.t: Helmholtz developed Young's three-receptor idea into the Young-Helmholtz trichromatic theory of colour vision.
He also proposed the place theory of hearing and unconscious inference in perception.

wrong.a: The JND belongs to Weber and Fechner, not Helmholtz.
wrong.c: The dynamic unconscious is Freud's; the trap is that Helmholtz spoke of unconscious inference, a different idea.
wrong.d: The law of effect is Thorndike's, a principle of learning.

q: Papillae is responsible for which sensory function?
who: Papillae and taste buds of the tongue

concept.t: Papillae are the bumps on the tongue that house the taste buds.
Fungiform, foliate and circumvallate papillae carry taste buds; filiform papillae lack taste buds and serve touch.

wrong.a: Smell receptors lie in the olfactory epithelium of the nose, not on the tongue.
wrong.b: Trap: only the filiform papillae serve touch, and they lack taste buds; papillae as a group are known for taste.
wrong.d: Vision uses the rods and cones of the retina, not the tongue.

q: Narendra turns around and around in a circle. When he stops, he feels like his head is spinning. What is responsible for this sensation?

concept.t: The semicircular canals of the inner ear are fluid-filled and sense rotation of the head.
When Narendra stops, the fluid in the canals keeps moving and bends the hair cells, signalling rotation in the opposite direction.

wrong.b: Proprioceptors report the position of the limbs, not rotation of the head.
wrong.c: The otolith organs detect tilt and linear acceleration, not spinning.
wrong.d: The crystals sit inside the otolith organs, so they too serve tilt and linear acceleration, not rotation.

q: What is a key feature of effective learning strategies for individuals with learning difficulties?

concept.t: Combining sight, sound, movement and touch strengthens learning, as the research on multisensory integration predicts.
Regular repetition then consolidates what was learned.

wrong.a: Relies on a single channel, which ignores the learner's difficulty.
wrong.d: Rote memorisation alone ignores the learner's difficulty.
